results.result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, an HIV reporter virus encoding a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the cell surface, enabling antibody-free magnetic cell sorting. The optimal construct (pNL4-3-ΔEnv-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR) expressed high levels of LNGFR early in infection (24 hr) in both CEM-T4s and primary CD4+ T cells, and routinely achieved ≥90% purity with ≤10% loss of infected cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C38 collectively demonstrate successful development and validation of the HIV-AFMACS system. The design strategy (C25-C27), construct selection based on expression kinetics (C28-C35), and performance metrics (C36-C37) are well-documented with experimental data and figures. The system addresses key methodological requirements for studying HIV infection in primary cells.

results.result: Time course proteomic analysis of HIV-infected primary CD4+ T cells quantitated 9070 cellular proteins across 10 conditions, revealing extensive T cell activation-dependent remodeling (29% of proteins changing >2-fold) and HIV-specific regulation of known accessory protein targets including tetherin (Vpu), SAMHD1 (not targeted by HIV-1), and substrates of Vif, Nef, Vpu, and Vpr.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C50 describe comprehensive time course proteomic data with appropriate controls for T cell activation. The quantitation of ~9000 proteins (C4, C39) and validation of known targets (C41-C47) with proper citations demonstrate technical rigor. Temporal expression patterns of viral proteins (C49-C50) are consistent with HIV biology.

results.result: Single time point proteomic analysis across three donors identified 650 HIV-dependent changes (q<0.05) in 8789 quantitated proteins, with 46% (297/650) attributable to known accessory protein effects. Downregulated pathways included DNA damage response/cell cycle (Vpr), cytidine deamination/PP2A activity (Vif), and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef), while upregulated pathways included lipid and sterol metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C62 provide reproducible findings across multiple donors with appropriate statistical thresholds (q<0.05). The pathway analysis (C57-C62) is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment and consistent with prior literature. The quantitative breakdown of accessory protein contributions (C56) demonstrates systematic analysis.

results.result: 192 proteins (30% of HIV-regulated proteins) were either not detected or not significantly regulated in CEM-T4 cells, including ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were validated by immunoblot and, based on temporal regulation patterns, identified as likely novel Vpr substrates specific to primary T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C7-C8, C69-C71, C77-C78 identify primary T cell-specific targets with multiple lines of evidence: proteomic detection (C69), quantitative depletion (C70), immunoblot validation (C71), and temporal profiling consistent with Vpr activity (C77). The inference about Vpr dependence (C77) is supported by comparison with known Vpr substrate ARID5B (C78).

results.result: DPH7 and FMR1 were identified as novel Vif-dependent targets. Both APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins were depleted in WT but not ΔVif virus-infected cells. Vif-dependent depletion of PPP2R5D was confirmed by immunoblot with functional validation through increased AURKB phosphorylation. DPH7 and FMR1 depletion was validated in both viral infection and single transgene expression systems, demonstrating Vif is necessary and sufficient for their degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C79-C91 provide comprehensive validation of novel Vif targets through multiple experimental approaches: comparative proteomics (WT vs ΔVif), immunoblot validation (C83, C88, C89), functional readout (C84), and necessity/sufficiency testing (C89-C90). The claim that these targets account for all significant Vif-dependent changes (C91) is well-supported by the systematic analysis.

results.result: Control experiments with lentivectors expressing SBP-ΔLNGFR alone or with Tat showed minimal perturbation (37/8518 proteins, 0.4%) and only 1/650 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) was also regulated by control vectors. No Tat-dependent changes were detected despite robust LTR transactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide critical negative controls demonstrating that the AFMACS system itself does not cause artifactual changes. The quantitative assessment (C66, C68) and lack of Tat effects (C67) despite functional transactivation strengthen confidence that observed changes are HIV-specific.

results.result: Temporal profiling distinguished Vpr substrates (near-maximal depletion by 24 hr in infected and partially in uninfected cells due to virion-packaged Vpr) from Vif/Nef/Vpu substrates (progressive depletion from 24-48 hr only in infected cells requiring de novo synthesis).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 demonstrate that temporal patterns can distinguish accessory protein mechanisms. The mechanistic explanation for Vpr effects (C73-C74, virion packaging) is supported by appropriate citations, and the observed patterns (C75-C76) are consistent with known HIV biology.

results.result: This study generated the first high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells. Primary T cell-specific proteins were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV than proteins detected in both cell types (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001). The depth of coverage (>90% proteins quantitated by ≥2 peptides) and high purity (>90% infected) maximized signal-to-noise ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97, C103-C106 establish the novelty and quality of the resource. The statistical comparison (C97) demonstrates biological significance of using primary cells. Technical metrics (C104-C106) support data quality claims, though the assertion of being 'first high coverage' (C95) should be qualified given the Kuo et al. 2018 study.

results.result: Comparison with a recent study (Kuo et al. 2018) that quantitated 7761 proteins at 96 hr post-infection showed that 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified in this study were obscured in that dataset, including depletion of ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7 and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 provide quantitative comparison with prior work, demonstrating advantages of the current approach. The specific enumeration of missed targets (C102) supports the claim of superior sensitivity, though the comparison is complicated by different time points (48 hr vs 96 hr) and viral constructs.

results.result: VSVg pseudotyping was used to enhance titers and enable synchronous infections, but may redirect viral entry and abrogate Env-dependent signaling. Only 1/650 HIV-dependent changes was observed in control lentivector-transduced cells, suggesting minimal false positives, though false negatives from absent Env-CD4 interactions remain possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 acknowledge important methodological limitations. The quantitative assessment of false positives (C109) is rigorous, while the discussion of potential false negatives (C110) appropriately qualifies the findings. The rationale for VSVg use (C107) is sound given the experimental goals.

results.result: The introduction establishes that viral infection causes host proteome remodeling through direct viral effects, secondary effects, or host countermeasures, which can be differentiated by temporal profiling. Primary T cells are superior to transformed cell lines (like CEM-T4) because accessory proteins Vif, Nef, and Vpu are required in primary but not many transformed T cells, and high MOI experiments may not reflect single provirus effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C18 provide appropriate background and rationale from cited literature. The limitations of cell lines (C15-C17) and high MOI approaches (C18) justify the experimental design. These are well-established concepts in the field supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: AFMACS-based selection offers advantages over conventional methods: it is faster, simpler, and more scalable than FACS, and avoids artifacts from antibody-mediated receptor cross-linking or bead internalization because cells are released with biotin.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe methodological advantages supported by appropriate citations. These are comparative statements about technique rather than novel findings, but provide important context for why AFMACS was chosen.

results.result: Temporal profiling is well-suited for identifying direct viral targets, and accessory proteins account for most proteomic remodeling in HIV-infected cells. Downregulated proteins correlate well between primary T cells and cell lines due to abundant direct accessory protein targets, while upregulated proteins show less concordance, possibly reflecting indirect, cell-type-specific transcriptional effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 provide interpretive synthesis of the results. The distinction between downregulated (direct) and upregulated (indirect) changes (C113-C115) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanistic explanation for upregulated proteins (C115) remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Novel HIV targets identified in this study (FMR1, ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7) impact processes relevant for HIV replication including virus infectivity, inflammatory signaling, T cell activation, and translational fidelity, underscoring the value of unbiased systems-level approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C121 place findings in functional context using appropriate citations. While the specific roles of these proteins in HIV infection require further investigation, their known functions (C117-C120) in relevant processes are well-documented. The concluding statement (C121) appropriately emphasizes the discovery aspect.

results.result: Some reported Vpu/Nef substrates may be downregulated from the plasma membrane without protein degradation (e.g., NTB-A, CCR7) or may have expression prevented without reduction below baseline (e.g., ICAM-1/3), explaining why not all reported targets were detected in this proteomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 provide reasonable explanations for discrepancies with prior literature, supported by appropriate citations. This acknowledges that whole-cell proteomics may miss membrane redistribution or prevention of upregulation, which are valid limitations of the approach.

results.result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, a reporter virus encoding a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the cell surface that enables antibody-free magnetic cell sorting (AFMACS) of infected cells. The optimal construct (pNL4-3-ΔEnv-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR) expressed the marker early in infection and achieved ≥90% purity with ≤10% loss in both CEM-T4s and primary CD4+ T cells.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers praised the technical innovation of HIV-AFMACS. Reviewer 2 specifically highlighted 'the technical innovation' and 'the emphasis on primary cells' as strengths. Reviewer 3 stated the study is 'compelling, appropriately controlled' with no concerns raised about the AFMACS methodology itself. The editors noted all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set using primary CD4+ T cells' and found it 'technically innovative.'

results.result: Using HIV-AFMACS, the authors quantitated approximately 9000 cellular proteins across multiple donors in primary CD4+ T cells, generating the first high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells. The depth of coverage reduced quantitation variability and the high purity (>90% infected) maximized effect sizes, resulting in high signal-to-noise ratios.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised the dataset quality and scope. Reviewer 1 called it 'the largest data set in using primary CD4+ T cells to-date' and 'technically sound.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the depth and stringency of the mass spec data obtained' and noted 'the interactive spreadsheet that provides an easy-to-access and expansive resource.' The editors stated all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set' and that it provides 'an easy-to-access resource for the community.'

results.result: Among 650 HIV-dependent protein changes (q<0.05), known accessory protein-dependent changes characterized in T cell lines accounted for 297/650 (46%) of proteins regulated in primary T cells, including 175/299 (59%) of decreased proteins. Accessory proteins (Vpr, Vif, Nef, Vpu) account for much of the proteomic remodeling, with pathways including DNA damage response/cell cycle (Vpr), cytidine deamination/PP2A activity (Vif), and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted 'over half of the 600+ changes were dependent on Vpr and Vif/Nef/Vpu' as a key observation. Reviewer 3 stated the study is 'appropriately controlled' and the results are 'of significant interest to the community.' No reviewer questioned the identification or quantification of accessory protein effects.

results.result: The authors identified novel Vif-dependent targets DPH7 and FMR1 in primary T cells. Both proteins showed profound Vif-dependent depletion confirmed by proteomics in CEM-T4s and primary cells, and validated by immunoblot in cells infected with WT (but not ΔVif) virus and in cells transduced with Vif alone. Together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors, these account for all significant Vif-dependent changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expressed concern about 'novelty and overlap with prior and parallel work' and noted 'the functional significance of these interactions is unclear.' Reviewer 2 stated 'there is rather limited validation of new or interesting hits and no characterization of why they (in particular the highlighted factors DPH7 and FMR1) are affected by HIV or the roles they might play in viral or cellular biology.' While the depletion data are accepted, the biological significance remains questioned.

results.result: 192/650 (30%) proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells were either not detected or not significantly regulated in CEM-T4s, including ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were consistently depleted across all donors (fold change >2) and validated by immunoblot. Proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 praised 'the emphasis on primary cells' as a strength and noted the validation of ARID5A and PTPN22 'using immunoblot.' Reviewer 1 acknowledged these as 'novel cellular factors' though questioned their functional significance. Reviewer 3 found the study 'compelling' with results 'of significant interest to the community.' The identification and validation of primary cell-specific targets was accepted, though functional characterization was noted as limited.

results.result: Control experiments showed that expression of SBP-ΔLNGFR as a transgene or in lentiviral vectors caused minimal proteomic perturbations. Only 37/8518 (0.4%) proteins were significantly perturbed by control lentivectors, and only 1/650 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) was also regulated by control vectors. No Tat-dependent changes were identified despite robust LTR transactivation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised a critical concern: 'the authors did not include an evaluation of whether the expression of SBP-LNGFR and its display on the cell surface causes any changes in expression of cellular proteins, as an important negative control.' While the authors present control data (C65-C68), Reviewer 2 specifically requested evaluation of 'whether or not the potential effects of LNGFR overexpression and bead binding can truly be disregarded.' This suggests the control experiments may not fully address potential artifacts.

results.result: Time-course analysis revealed T cell activation caused extensive proteomic remodeling (29% of proteins changed >2-fold). Known restriction factors showed expected patterns: tetherin was upregulated by activation then depleted in infected cells (Vpu target), while SAMHD1 was depleted by activation independent of infection. Temporal profiling distinguished substrates of different accessory proteins based on characteristic kinetics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 found the study 'compelling, appropriately controlled' with no specific concerns about the temporal analysis. Reviewer 1 called it 'technically sound.' The temporal profiling approach builds on the authors' previous validated methodology (C12), and reviewers raised no objections to these findings. Reviewer 3's question about T cell activation (point 7) sought discussion rather than challenging the data.

results.result: Vpr-dependent changes from CEM-T4s were recapitulated in primary T cells, with 33 newly described Vpr substrates quantitated and 32 decreased in abundance. ARID5A and PTPN22 likely represent novel Vpr substrates based on temporal patterns, consistent with ARID5B being a conserved Vpr target.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted this represents 'overlap with prior and parallel work' citing 'a sister paper (Greenwood, 2018) that describes the Vpr downregulated proteome.' However, the validation of these targets in primary cells (the natural target) was not challenged. Reviewer 3 stated results are 'of significant interest to the community' without raising concerns about the Vpr findings.

results.result: Marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism were observed in HIV-infected cells. Similar effects have been reported in T cell lines at the transcriptional level and attributed to Nef expression, and several proteins in these pathways are indirectly regulated by Vpr.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenged these findings. The lipid metabolism changes are presented as confirmatory of previous transcriptional studies (C61) and consistent with known Vpr effects (C62). Reviewers accepted these observations without comment, treating them as supporting rather than novel findings.

results.result: Compared to previous studies, this work provides superior coverage. Previous temporal proteomic analyses had limited coverage (<2000 proteins) and did not detect known targets. A recent study (Kuo et al. 2018) quantitated 7761 proteins but 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified here were obscured in that study, including ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7 and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted the superior quality of this dataset. Reviewer 1 acknowledged it as 'the largest data set in using primary CD4+ T cells to-date.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the depth and stringency of the mass spec data obtained.' The editors noted all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set.' The comparison to previous studies was not challenged.

results.result: The authors used Env-deficient proviral backbone with VSVg pseudotyping to enhance titers, avoid Env-dependent cytotoxicity, enable synchronous infections, and bypass co-receptor-dependent targeting. VSVg redirects entry to an endocytic pathway and may abrogate Env-dependent signaling. The absence of Env-CD4/co-receptor interactions may have resulted in underestimation of proteomic changes (false negatives).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised significant concerns: 'it is unfortunate that ΔEnv viruses were chosen for the analysis considering the large impact Env-CD4/CoR binding can have on primary T cell responses' and 'it seems reasonable that their viruses could have been pseudotyped with wild-type Envelope proteins instead of VSV-G.' Reviewer 2 requested 'further discussion of this issue' and noted it would have been 'even more compelling to compare R5 vs. X4 or TF to non-TF glycoproteins.' While the authors acknowledge potential false negatives (C110), the experimental design choice is questioned.

results.result: AFMACS-based selection offers advantages over conventional methods: it is fast, simple, scalable, antibody-free, and selected cells are released from beads with biotin. Conventional antibody-based methods risk altering cell behavior through receptor cross-linking or bead internalization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the technical advantages of AFMACS. Reviewer 2 noted 'the technical innovation' as a strength. However, Reviewer 2 also stated 'the authors should also explain the limitations of AFMACS-selection more thoroughly,' suggesting the discussion of advantages should be balanced with limitations. The method's advantages are accepted but may be overstated without adequate discussion of limitations.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on HIV-AFMACS system development and validation (C1-C38). Both evaluations find the technical innovation compelling and well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes experimental documentation while peer reviewers highlight innovation and use of primary cells as key strengths.

Significant disagreement on Vif target validation (C6, C79-C91). OpenEval finds comprehensive validation through multiple experimental approaches and considers claims well-supported. Peer reviewers accept the depletion data but express concern about 'limited validation' and 'unclear functional significance,' rating as UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on superior dataset quality compared to prior work (C100-C102). Both evaluations accept the quantitative comparison and acknowledge this as the largest primary CD4+ T cell dataset to date without challenge.

Agreement on AFMACS technical advantages (C92-C94). Both accept the methodological benefits, though peer reviewers note the discussion should be balanced with more thorough explanation of limitations.

Disagreement on adequacy of negative controls (C65-C68, C109). OpenEval finds controls demonstrate no artifactual changes and rates as SUPPORTED. Peer Reviewer 2 raises critical concern that LNGFR overexpression and bead binding effects were not adequately evaluated, rating as UNCERTAIN.

Disagreement on VSVg pseudotyping limitation (C107-C108, C110). OpenEval finds the rationale sound and limitations appropriately acknowledged. Peer Reviewer 2 questions the experimental design choice, stating it was 'unfortunate' and suggesting wild-type Envelope would have been more compelling, rating as UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on identification of primary T cell-specific targets (C7-C8, C63-C64, C69-C71, C77-C78, C96-C97). Both evaluations accept the validation data and novelty of findings in primary cells, though peer reviewers note limited functional characterization.

Agreement on temporal proteomic profiling and validation (C40-C50, C72-C76). Both find the time course data technically sound and appropriately controlled. OpenEval emphasizes validation of known targets while peer reviewers find the approach compelling without specific concerns.

Agreement on dataset quality and resource value (C95-C97, C103-C106). Both evaluations praise the magnitude, depth, and accessibility of the data. Peer reviewers emphasize the interactive spreadsheet as an important community resource. OpenEval notes the 'first high coverage' claim should be qualified.

Agreement on reproducibility and pathway analysis (C5, C51-C59). Both evaluations accept the multi-donor findings and statistical thresholds without challenge. Peer reviewers note accessory protein effects as key observations of significant community interest.

Agreement on temporal pattern analysis distinguishing accessory protein mechanisms (C72-C76). Both find the mechanistic explanations supported by appropriate citations and consistent with HIV biology. Peer reviewers accept without specific concerns.

Agreement on lipid metabolism pathway findings (C60-C62). Both evaluations accept these observations as confirmatory of previous transcriptional studies. Peer reviewers treat as supporting rather than novel findings without challenge.

Agreement on comprehensive proteomic data quality (C3-C4, C39). Both evaluations praise the quantitation of ~9000 proteins and technical rigor. Peer reviewers emphasize depth and stringency while OpenEval highlights validation of known targets.

Agreement on Vpr substrate validation (C78). Both accept ARID5B as a known Vpr target used for comparison. Peer Reviewer 1 notes overlap with parallel work (Greenwood 2018) but validation in primary cells is not challenged.

Agreement on interpretation of direct vs indirect effects (C112). Both evaluations accept the distinction between downregulated and upregulated changes. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this framework without challenge.

OpenEval finds background and rationale claims (C9-C18) well-supported by cited literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific background claims, though peer reviewers implicitly accept the rationale by praising the emphasis on primary cells.

OpenEval finds interpretive synthesis (C111-C115) supported, noting mechanistic explanations for upregulated proteins remain somewhat speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation directly addresses these interpretive claims.

OpenEval finds functional context claims (C116-C121) supported with appropriate citations, emphasizing discovery aspect. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific functional context claims.
OpenEval finds explanations for discrepancies with prior literature (C98-C99) reasonable and well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation directly addresses these reconciliation claims.
